reference_opening.argument: This video is scam content because it presents a smart-contract and flash-loan method as an earning opportunity, claiming possible four-to-eight-times returns and a seven-times result. It directs viewers to connect a wallet, send about $200 of MATIC to a contract, deploy it, and call its flashloan function. The risk disclaimer and lack of independent verification qualify the claims but do not remove the solicitation and return relationship.

opening.argument: Judge the return claim in the context of the creator's own qualifications. He says, “This worked for me. But TRY IT AT YOUR OWN RISK!” and acknowledges that the method “probably won't work forever.” Those are material limits on the claim: he presents a reported personal result, not a promise that another wallet will produce the same one. Even his larger-return prediction is conditional, “if we're lucky.” The more defensible reading is a risky technical demonstration whose outcome viewers are expressly warned not to assume.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opening rightly identifies a funding instruction, but that alone does not establish a guaranteed-return offer. The stated purpose of the transfer is “gas fee for all swaps,” while the creator explicitly says to try the method at one's own risk. The seven-times figure is his reported result, not evidence that he promises every viewer that result.

This worked for me. But TRY IT AT YOUR OWN RISK!

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The warning does not undo the concrete earning pitch. The creator instructs viewers to send $200 of MATIC to the contract, then call its flashloan function, and presents a seven-times return as the result. Conditional wording limits certainty, but it does not turn a funded-contract profit workflow into merely a discussion of risk.

opening.argument: The central presentation is a walkthrough of development tools and a claimed transaction sequence. The speaker introduces “educational information” for newcomers, starts a fresh Remix workspace, names a Solidity file, and explains the compiler setting. The description likewise lays out setup and compilation steps. A judge can recognize that the narrator makes an ambitious profit claim without treating every programming demonstration involving a wallet as a solicitation; the cited material shows what he says he did, but does not independently establish what the contract does or whether its claimed result can be reproduced.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The reference opening treats the linked code and wallet connection as evidence of an earning solicitation. They are also ordinary components of the tool demonstration the narrator describes: he explains that Remix is used to compile and interface with contracts. His mention of an attack against AAVE describes the proposed method; the description alone does not verify an AAVE interaction or the claimed return.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The tutorial format is real, but the tutorial's endpoint matters. It directs viewers to fund the contract and invoke its flashloan function; the speaker then calls the result a seven-times return. Showing compiler settings does not make those funding instructions and profit claims incidental.

citations.quote: Send $200 of MATIC to the contract for gas fee for all swaps
Call 'flashloan' function in Remix.
So, a little over $200 to $1496. I just did a 7x.

opening.argument: The described payment is framed as a transaction cost for swaps, not as a purchase of a managed investment: the instructions call it “gas fee for all swaps.” The viewer is told to create a file, deploy a contract and call a function through Remix. Those steps may be risky, and the reported profit deserves skepticism. But these sources do not establish that the creator takes custody of viewers' funds, asks for wallet credentials, or pays returns for recruiting others. The evidence supports scrutiny of an unverified, self-directed contract procedure; it does not, by itself, establish those additional scam mechanisms.

rebuttal.rebuttal: Calling the transfer “funding” does not show who ultimately controls the deployed contract or where its assets go. The description instructs viewers to get the contract address from Remix and describes the MATIC as swap gas. The opening's return relationship warrants caution, but the cited instructions do not resolve custody or independently verify the alleged profits.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The case does not require proof of credential theft, recruitment, or who ultimately controls the contract. The creator supplies contract code, tells viewers to send $200 of MATIC to that contract, and reports turning a little over $200 into $1496. Calling the transfer a gas fee does not remove the direct connection he draws between funding the contract and earning a return.
